abstract: Single-trial decoding of semantic processing from EEG is used in cognitive neuroscience, brain-computer interfaces and EEG-to-text research. Because single trials are noisy, the choice of features can determine how much information a decoder uses. Yet these fields use different features that have not been compared systematically: event-related potential studies decode the voltage time course (the waveform), EEG-to-text studies mostly the power of oscillations in frequency bands. We crossed four feature-processing choices--signal representation (waveform or band power), time window, normalization and channel set--into 640 configurations and decoded whether a stimulus fitted its semantic context in three tasks: visual word pairs, objects in visual scenes, and words in spoken sentences (40 participants per task). Eleven pre-specified comparisons were tested jointly. The signal representation had by far the largest effect on accuracy (mean generalized eta squared = 0.165, an order of magnitude above any other effect). Averaged over tasks and other choices, balanced accuracy was 56.6% with the waveform and 50.6% with theta-band power (chance, 50%), and adding band power to the waveform lowered accuracy by 1.8 percentage points, in every task. Both effects replicated, and were larger, in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants from three sites. Neither a finer time-frequency decomposition including the delta band (2-4 Hz) nor a different way of combining power with the waveform changed this conclusion, whereas the time window, normalization and channel set mattered little. For semantic decoding from single EEG trials, the waveform carries the information, and band power does not add to it.
